claims.text: Overall wear resistance is governed by coating grain size.
Microscopic deformation during sliding is governed by coating grain size.
Overall wear resistance is governed by substrate surface roughness.
Microscopic deformation during sliding is governed by substrate surface roughness.
The modified coating condition has a grain size of 10 μm.
The modified coating condition has a substrate surface roughness of 0.5 μm.
The baseline coating has a grain size of 20 μm.
The baseline substrate surface roughness is 1.0 μm.
Reducing grain size from 20 μm to 10 μm reduces stress concentration.
Reducing substrate surface roughness from 1.0 μm to 0.5 μm improves coating-substrate adhesion.
Reduced stress concentration and improved coating-substrate adhesion increase wear resistance.
Reduced stress concentration and improved coating-substrate adhesion reduce microscopic deformation.
The modified condition will increase wear resistance by 20% relative to the baseline.
The modified condition will reduce microscopic deformation by 30% relative to the baseline.
The predictions apply for coating thicknesses from 5 μm to 20 μm.
The specified sliding conditions are a speed of 0.1 m/s and a normal load of 10 N.
A wear-rate increase greater than 10% or a microscopic-deformation increase greater than 20% relative to baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated intervention varies temperature and coating thickness, whereas the hypothesized controlled mediator change is grain size and substrate roughness. The design therefore does not explicitly manipulate the variables whose baseline-to-modified changes are claimed to cause the outcome.

The prediction requires a 20% wear-resistance increase and 30% deformation reduction, but the falsification rule tolerates unchanged performance and even smaller adverse changes. Thus failure to obtain the predicted directional improvements would not necessarily falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
